claim: Cohesin helps mediate sister chromatid cohesion.
source: Cohesin helps mediate sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome condensation, DNA repair, and transcription regulation.
evidence: This is a well-established function of cohesin stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cohesin helps mediate chromosome condensation.
source: Cohesin helps mediate sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome condensation, DNA repair, and transcription regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cohesin helps mediate DNA repair.
source: Cohesin helps mediate sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome condensation, DNA repair, and transcription regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cohesin helps mediate transcription regulation.
source: Cohesin helps mediate sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome condensation, DNA repair, and transcription regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Both cohesin's head and hinge domains are proximal to DNA.
source: Our results suggest that both cohesin's head and hinge domains are proximal to DNA, and cohesin structure is dynamic with differential folding of its coiled coil regions to generate butterfly confirmations.
evidence: This is supported by proximity biotinylation experiments with DNA-tethered BirA shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cohesin structure is dynamic with differential folding of its coiled coil regions to generate butterfly conformations.
source: Our results suggest that both cohesin's head and hinge domains are proximal to DNA, and cohesin structure is dynamic with differential folding of its coiled coil regions to generate butterfly confirmations.
evidence: This is supported by cis-biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 2C demonstrating multiple AviTags can be biotinylated by BirA at different positions.

claim: Cohesins form ordered clusters on and off DNA.
source: This method also reveals that cohesins form ordered clusters on and off DNA.
evidence: This is supported by trans-biotinylation experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The levels of cohesin clusters are cell cycle-regulated.
source: The levels of cohesin clusters and their distribution on chromosomes are cell cycle-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation experiments at different cell cycle stages shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The distribution of cohesin clusters on chromosomes is cell cycle-regulated.
source: The levels of cohesin clusters and their distribution on chromosomes are cell cycle-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5 demonstrating different distributions in S phase versus mid-M phase.

claim: Cohesin clustering is likely necessary for cohesion maintenance.
source: Cohesin clustering is likely necessary for cohesion maintenance because clustering and maintenance uniquely require the same subset of cohesin domains and the auxiliary cohesin factor Pds5p.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that mutations blocking clustering (mcd1-V137K, mcd1-Q266, smc3-D667) also block cohesion maintenance, and Pds5p depletion blocks both clustering and cohesion maintenance.

claim: Clustering and cohesion maintenance uniquely require the same subset of cohesin domains.
source: Cohesin clustering is likely necessary for cohesion maintenance because clustering and maintenance uniquely require the same subset of cohesin domains and the auxiliary cohesin factor Pds5p.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing that mutations in specific domains (Mcd1p linker, Mcd1p ROCC, Smc3p hinge) block both clustering and cohesion maintenance.

claim: Clustering and cohesion maintenance uniquely require the auxiliary cohesin factor Pds5p.
source: Cohesin clustering is likely necessary for cohesion maintenance because clustering and maintenance uniquely require the same subset of cohesin domains and the auxiliary cohesin factor Pds5p.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in Figure 7E-F showing Pds5p depletion blocks clustering, and by citations showing Pds5p is required for cohesion maintenance.

claim: SMC complexes tether and fold chromosomes by two activities.
source: SMC complexes tether and fold chromosomes by two activities.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: SMC complexes can tether together two regions of DNA, either within a single chromosome or between sister chromatids.
source: First, they can tether together two regions of DNA, either within a single chromosome or between sister chromatids (Hassler et al., 2018; Onn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By combining tethering activity with their ability to translocate along DNA, SMC complexes can extrude DNA loops in vivo and in vitro.
source: Second, by combining this tethering activity with their ability to translocate along DNA, SMC complexes can also extrude DNA loops (loop extrusion) in vivo and in vitro (Wang et al., 2017; Ganji et al., 2018; Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating loop extrusion.

claim: All SMC complexes have a dimer of two evolutionarily related proteins called Smc at their core.
source: At their core, all SMC complexes have a dimer of two evolutionarily related proteins, which are called Smc (Strunnikov et al., 1993; Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Strunnikov et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies identifying SMC proteins.

claim: Each Smc subunit has two globular domains, a head domain and a hinge domain, separated by a long 50-nm coiled coil.
source: Each Smc subunit has two globular domains, a head domain and a hinge domain, separated by a long 50-nm coiled coil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMC protein structure.

claim: Smc subunits dimerize by two distinct interactions, one between the two heads and another between the two hinges.
source: Smc subunits dimerize by two distinct interactions, one between the two heads and another between the two hinges.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMC protein structure.

claim: The Smc dimers can achieve multiple conformations in vitro, including rings, rods, or butterflies.
source: The separation of head and hinge dimers by their intervening long coiled coils allows the Smc dimers to achieve multiple conformations in vitro, including rings, rods, or butterflies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A showing these conformations and by citations in the text.

claim: The butterfly conformations result from bending of the coiled coils of the SMC subunits bringing the hinge and head domains in close proximity.
source: The butterfly conformations result from bending of the coiled coils of the SMC subunits bringing the hinge and head domains in close proximity (Hirano et al., 2001; Soh et al., 2015; Bürmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The Smc subunits act as scaffolds to bind non-Smc proteins.
source: The Smc subunits also act as scaffolds to bind non-Smc proteins (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Cohesin was originally discovered in budding yeast because it mediates cohesion between sister chromatids.
source: One SMC complex, called cohesin, was originally discovered in budding yeast because it mediates cohesion between sister chromatids (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: The subunits of budding yeast cohesin (Smc1p, Smc3p, Mcd1p/Scc1p, and Scc3p) are conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: The subunits of budding yeast cohesin (Figure 1A; Smc1p and Smc3p, and the non-SMC subunits Mcd1p/Scc1p and Scc3p) are conserved throughout eukaryotes (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997; Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is established knowledge.

claim: Sister chromatid cohesion is essential for chromosome segregation in mitosis and meiosis.
source: Sister chromatid cohesion is essential for chromosome segregation in mitosis and meiosis (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997; Klein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: Cohesin is important for chromosome condensation.
source: Subsequently, cohesin was also shown to be important for chromosome condensation, efficient DNA repair, and the regulation of gene expression (Guacci et al., 1997; Ström et al., 2004; Wood et al., 2010; Dorsett and Ström, 2012; Lopez-Serra et al., 2013; Bloom et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Lamothe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cohesin is important for efficient DNA repair.
source: Subsequently, cohesin was also shown to be important for chromosome condensation, efficient DNA repair, and the regulation of gene expression (Guacci et al., 1997; Ström et al., 2004; Wood et al., 2010; Dorsett and Ström, 2012; Lopez-Serra et al., 2013; Bloom et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Lamothe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cohesin is important for the regulation of gene expression.
source: Subsequently, cohesin was also shown to be important for chromosome condensation, efficient DNA repair, and the regulation of gene expression (Guacci et al., 1997; Ström et al., 2004; Wood et al., 2010; Dorsett and Ström, 2012; Lopez-Serra et al., 2013; Bloom et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Lamothe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations in cohesin subunits are thought to drive cancer.
source: Mutations in cohesin subunits are thought to drive cancer and cause age-dependent congenital disabilities and developmental disorders (Brooker and Berkowitz, 2014; Romero-Pérez et al., 2019; Ogawa, 2019; Watrin et al., 2016; Chiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cohesin mutations in disease.

claim: Mutations in cohesin subunits cause age-dependent congenital disabilities and developmental disorders.
source: Mutations in cohesin subunits are thought to drive cancer and cause age-dependent congenital disabilities and developmental disorders (Brooker and Berkowitz, 2014; Romero-Pérez et al., 2019; Ogawa, 2019; Watrin et al., 2016; Chiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cohesin mutations in disease.

claim: Cohesion establishment requires the Scc2p/Scc4p complex to load cohesin on one sister chromatid.
source: First, the Scc2p/Scc4p complex loads cohesin on one sister chromatid (Ciosk et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on cohesin loading.

claim: Cohesin is acetylated by Eco1p, which promotes tethering of the second sister chromatid.
source: Then cohesin is acetylated by Eco1p, which promotes tethering of the second sister chromatid (Tóth et al., 1999; Skibbens et al., 1999; Unal et al., 2008; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Guacci and Koshland, 2012; Çamdere et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Eco1p and cohesin acetylation.

claim: Cohesin acetylation helps to maintain cohesion by preventing cohesin from being removed by Wpl1p from chromosomes.
source: Cohesin acetylation helps to maintain cohesion by preventing cohesin from being removed by Wpl1p from chromosomes (Kueng et al., 2006; Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Lopez-Serra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Wpl1p and cohesin acetylation.

claim: Cohesion maintenance is promoted by the cohesin binding protein Pds5p.
source: Cohesion maintenance is also promoted by the cohesin binding protein called Pds5p (Hartman et al., 2000; Tanaka et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002; Noble et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Pds5p function.

claim: Pds5p facilitates efficient Eco1p-dependent acetylation of cohesin, thereby inhibits Wpl1p-dependent cohesin release.
source: Pds5p facilitates efficient Eco1p-dependent acetylation of cohesin, thereby inhibits Wpl1p-dependent cohesin release (Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on Pds5p function.

claim: Pds5p maintains cohesion by a second unknown mechanism that is independent of Wpl1p inhibition.
source: In addition, Pds5p maintains cohesion by a second unknown mechanism that is independent of Wpl1p inhibition (Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study showing Pds5p has Wpl1p-independent functions.

claim: Cohesin rings have been observed by electron microscopy and liquid atomic force microscopy.
source: Cohesin rings have been observed by electron microscopy (EM) and liquid atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Hirano et al., 2001; Anderson et al., 2002; Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Rings have been inferred to exist in vivo from experiments showing cohesin's ability to topologically entrap DNA.
source: Rings have also been inferred to exist in vivo from experiments showing cohesin's ability to topologically entrap DNA (Haering et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on DNA entrapment.

claim: Rods have been seen by EM and inferred to exist in vivo from cross-linking experiments.
source: Rods have been seen by EM and inferred to exist in vivo from cross-linking experiments (Anderson et al., 2002; Soh et al., 2015); however, rods were not observed in liquid AFM images (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging and cross-linking studies.

claim: Rods were not observed in liquid AFM images.
source: Rods have been seen by EM and inferred to exist in vivo from cross-linking experiments (Anderson et al., 2002; Soh et al., 2015); however, rods were not observed in liquid AFM images (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an AFM study.

claim: A butterfly conformation forms in vitro by bending of the cohesin coiled coil at the elbow.
source: A butterfly conformation forms in vitro by bending of the cohesin coiled coil at the elbow (Bürmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: The butterfly structure is extremely rare in negatively stained electron microscopies.
source: While the butterfly structure is extremely rare in negatively stained electron microscopies, it was more prevalent in liquid AFM images (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an imaging study.

claim: The butterfly structure was more prevalent in liquid AFM images.
source: While the butterfly structure is extremely rare in negatively stained electron microscopies, it was more prevalent in liquid AFM images (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an AFM study.

claim: The existence of the butterfly structure in vitro is supported by the detection of interactions between purified Scc3p and the hinge in recent cryo-EM images of cohesin.
source: The existence of a butterfly structure in vitro is also supported by the detection of interactions between purified Scc3p and the hinge in recent cryo-EM images of cohesin (Murayama and Uhlmann, 2015; Shi et al., 2020; Higashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM studies.

claim: The existence of the butterfly structure in vivo has been inferred from imaging and functional interactions of the hinge and the head-bound Pds5p.
source: In vivo, the existence of this structure has been inferred from imaging and functional interactions of the hinge and the head-bound Pds5p (Mc Intyre et al., 2007; Eng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging and functional studies.

claim: In two recent single molecular studies, the photobleaching of fluorescently tagged cohesin came to different conclusions about whether cohesin bound to DNA as monomers or dimers.
source: In two recent single molecular studies, the photobleaching of fluorescently tagged cohesin came to different conclusions about whether cohesin bound to DNA as monomers or dimers (Kim et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two single-molecule studies with conflicting results.

claim: Studies disagree about the presence of cohesin dimers in cells tested by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: In vivo, the presence of dimers in cells was tested by co-immunoprecipitation. Other studies also disagree about the presence of dimers (Zhang et al., 2008; Haering et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies with conflicting results on cohesin dimers.

claim: Recent in vivo studies revealed functional complementation between distinct cohesin complexes that are individually defective on their own.
source: More recent in vivo studies revealed the functional complementation between distinct cohesin complexes that are individually defective on their own (Eng et al., 2015; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional complementation studies.

claim: Functional complementation between distinct cohesin complexes could be best explained by the clustering of cohesins.
source: This complementation could be best explained by the clustering of cohesins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional complementation data cited.

claim: Proximity biotinylation is a method that exploits the ability of the bacterial enzyme BirA to recognize a 15 amino acid AviTag and add a biotin moiety to a lysine residue within the AviTag.
source: Proximity biotinylation is a method that exploits the ability of the bacterial enzyme, BirA, to recognize a 15 amino acid AviTag and add a biotin moiety to a lysine residue within the AviTag (Fernández-Suárez et al., 2008; Branon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the proximity biotinylation method.

claim: In vivo, biotinylation of the AviTag is enhanced when the AviTag and BirA are fused to two interacting partners that place the BirA and AviTag in proximity.
source: In vivo, biotinylation of the AviTag is enhanced when the AviTag and BirA are fused to two interacting partners that place the BirA and AviTag in proximity.
evidence: This is a principle of the proximity biotinylation method.

claim: The BirA and AviTag partners must be in very close proximity to generate AviTag biotinylation because this biotinylation only occurs when the AviTag binds to the active site of BirA.
source: Importantly, the BirA and AviTag partners must be in very close proximity to generate AviTag biotinylation because this biotinylation only occurs when the AviTag binds to the active site of BirA.
evidence: This is a principle of the proximity biotinylation method based on the mechanism of BirA.

claim: All four Smc3p-AviTag reporters are functional in vivo.
source: First, we showed that all the Smc3p-AviTag reporters and Smc3p-BirA were functional in vivo. Strains bearing any of these SMC3-AviTag or SMC3-BirA genes as the sole source grew at similar rates as the wild-type strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by growth assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Smc3p-BirA constructs are functional in vivo.
source: First, we showed that all the Smc3p-AviTag reporters and Smc3p-BirA were functional in vivo. Strains bearing any of these SMC3-AviTag or SMC3-BirA genes as the sole source grew at similar rates as the wild-type strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by growth assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All four Smc3p-AviTag reporters are biotinylated to the same extent by freely diffusible nucleoplasmic BirA.
source: Furthermore, we showed that all four Smc3p-AviTag reporters are biotinylated to the same extent by freely diffusible nucleoplasmic BirA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The western blot-based assay is quantitative because the Western signal of the Smc3p-AviTag reporter showed a linear response to serial dilutions of Smc3-AviTag protein.
source: We also showed that our western blot-based assay was quantitative because the Western signal of the Smc3p-AviTag reporter showed a linear response to serial dilutions of Smc3-AviTag protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The majority of the biotinylation observed for Smc3p in the Smc3p-Smc1p heterodimers reflects the interaction of the partner domains in cis.
source: We conclude that the majority of the biotinylation that we observe for Smc3p in the Smc3p-Smc1p heterodimers reflects the interaction of the partner domains in cis.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of cis and trans biotinylation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The heterodimer is structurally dynamic, transitioning between multiple conformations in vivo.
source: The promiscuous cis-biotinylation pattern of the three AviTags by the hinge BirA strongly suggests that the heterodimer is structurally dynamic, transitioning between multiple conformations in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the biotinylation pattern shown in Figure 2C where multiple AviTags are biotinylated by hinge BirA.

claim: The coiled coil between the hinge and elbow is flexible, allowing the hinge domain to bind to the elbow-proximal coiled coil, coiled coil, or head domains.
source: We suggest that the coiled coil between the hinge and elbow is flexible, allowing the hinge domain to bind to the elbow-proximal coiled coil, coiled coil, or head domains, reflecting multiple distinct butterfly conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the biotinylation pattern in Figure 2C.

claim: The coiled coil between the head and elbow is stiffer than the coiled coil between the hinge and elbow.
source: We conclude that the head BirA, unlike the hinge BirA, must be constrained to prevent its interaction with the elbow reporter. We suggest that the coiled coil between the head and elbow is stiffer than the coiled coil between the hinge and elbow, thereby limiting the ability of the head domain to interact with the elbow.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential biotinylation of the elbow reporter by head BirA versus hinge BirA shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The fully assembled cohesin complex, like the heterodimers, is capable of forming multiple butterfly conformations in vivo.
source: These results are consistent with the conclusion that the fully assembled cohesin complex, like the heterodimers, is capable of forming multiple butterfly conformations in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar biotinylation patterns in G1 and mid-M shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The head and the hinge domains are more proximal to chromosomal DNA than the elbow and the CC.
source: These results suggest that the head and the hinge domains are more proximal to chromosomal DNA than the elbow and the CC.
evidence: This is supported by differential biotinylation by DNA-tethered BirA shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cohesin binding to DNA enhanced head and hinge reporter biotinylation four-fold.
source: Cohesin binding to DNA enhanced head and hinge reporter biotinylation four-fold.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of biotinylation with and without Scc2p depletion shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The biotinylation of elbow reporter was enhanced only two-fold by cohesin binding to DNA.
source: The biotinylation of elbow reporter was enhanced only two-fold, whereas head-proximal coiled coil reporter biotinylation was not enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of biotinylation with and without Scc2p depletion shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Head-proximal coiled coil reporter biotinylation was not enhanced by cohesin binding to DNA.
source: The biotinylation of elbow reporter was enhanced only two-fold, whereas head-proximal coiled coil reporter biotinylation was not enhanced.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of biotinylation with and without Scc2p depletion shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Trans-biotinylation of the head and hinge reporters increased 7.5-fold in S phase arrested cells to 45%.
source: Trans-biotinylation of the head and hinge reporters increased 7.5-fold in S phase (hydroxyurea) arrested cells to 45% and four-fold in mid-M phase (nocodazole) arrested cells to 25% (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Trans-biotinylation of the head and hinge reporters increased four-fold in mid-M phase arrested cells to 25%.
source: Trans-biotinylation of the head and hinge reporters increased 7.5-fold in S phase (hydroxyurea) arrested cells to 45% and four-fold in mid-M phase (nocodazole) arrested cells to 25% (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cohesin efficiently clusters in vivo.
source: These results show that cohesin efficiently clusters in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by trans-biotinylation data in Figure 4C showing high levels of biotinylation.

claim: The trans-biotinylation of the CC reporter by the BirA in the head of another cohesin molecule remained low in S and mid-M phase arrested cells.
source: The trans-biotinylation of the CC reporter by the BirA in the head of another cohesin molecule remained low in S and mid-M phase arrested cells.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cohesin clustering is consistent with an ordered manner that enables head–head and head–hinge interactions between different cohesin molecules, but disfavors interaction between CC of one cohesin complex and the head of another cohesin.
source: These results are consistent with cohesin clustering in an ordered manner that enables head–head and head–hinge interactions between different cohesin molecules, but disfavors interaction between CC of one cohesin complex and the head of another cohesin.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential trans-biotinylation patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cohesin clustering is cell cycle-regulated, forming and peaking during S phase and then partially dissolving from G2 to M phase.
source: The results from arrested and cycling cells demonstrate that cohesin clustering is cell cycle-regulated, forming and peaking during S phase and then partially dissolving from G2 to M phase.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data during cell cycle progression shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The presence of clusters between S phase to mid-M correlates with the time when cohesion is established and maintained.
source: The presence of clusters between S phase to mid-M correlates with the time when cohesion is established and maintained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of clustering and known timing of cohesion establishment and maintenance.

claim: Both BirA-tagged and AviTag-tagged Smc3p robustly localized at previously identified CARs at the centromere, at a pericentric site, and on chromosomal arms to similar levels.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, both BirA-tagged and AviTag-tagged Smc3p, detected using anti-V5 and anti-MYC antibodies, respectively, robustly localized at previously identified CARs at the centromere, at a pericentric site, and on chromosomal arms to similar levels.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Biotinylated Smc3p reporter was detected at centromeres, at pericentric regions, and at arm CARs in S phase arrested cells.
source: We detected biotinylated Smc3p reporter at centromeres (e.g., CEN3), at pericentric regions, and at arm CARs using qPCR (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cohesin molecules at all CARs tested are clustering in S phase.
source: This similarity indicates that cohesin molecules at all CARs tested are clustering in S phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar ChIP signals between Smc3p-BirA and NLS-BirA conditions shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Smc3p-BirA-mediated trans-biotinylation of the Smc3p-AviTag reporter was robust at both CEN and pericentric regions in mid-M phase arrested cells.
source: As in S phase arrested cells, Smc3p-BirA-mediated trans-biotinylation of the Smc3p-AviTag reporter was robust at both CEN and pericentric regions.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The trans-biotinylation signal was greatly reduced at some arm CARs in mid-M phase arrested cells.
source: However, the trans-biotinylation signal was greatly reduced at some arm CARs but still above the signal in the negative control of cells lacking cells without BirA.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At other CARs, the trans-biotinylation signal was eliminated in mid-M phase arrested cells.
source: At other CARs, this signal was eliminated.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The levels of biotinylated Smc3p-AviTag reporter by the free nuclear BirA at CARs was very similar in S phase and mid-M arrested cells.
source: First, the levels of biotinylated Smc3p-AviTag reporter by the free nuclear BirA at CARs was very similar in S phase and mid-M arrested cells (Figure 5C, D), consistent with the robust binding of cohesin to CARs in HU and mid-M arrested cells reported previously (Blat and Kleckner, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The CARs continued to bind both Smc3p-AviTag and Smc3p-BirA in mid-M.
source: Second, the CARs continued to bind both Smc3p-AviTag and Smc3p-BirA in mid-M as evidenced by ChIP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cohesin clusters at arm CARs are downregulated in mid-M by mechanisms other than dissociating cohesin from chromosomes.
source: These results suggest that cohesin clusters at arm CARs are downregulated in mid-M by mechanisms other than dissociating cohesin from chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cohesin remains bound to CARs but trans-biotinylation is reduced.

claim: All peaks of cohesin clusters correlate with previously identified regions of cohesin binding.
source: All peaks of cohesin clusters correlate with previously identified regions of cohesin binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ChIP-seq data with previous studies shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Robust trans-biotinylation signal by Smc3p-BirA was observed at the centromeres and pericentric regions in mid-M arrested cells.
source: As predicted from the qPCR results, we observed robust trans-biotinylation signal by Smc3p-BirA at the centromeres and pericentric regions and much weaker signal or no signal at arm CARs (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Much weaker signal or no signal of trans-biotinylation by Smc3p-BirA was observed at arm CARs in mid-M arrested cells.
source: As predicted from the qPCR results, we observed robust trans-biotinylation signal by Smc3p-BirA at the centromeres and pericentric regions and much weaker signal or no signal at arm CARs (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The biotinylation signal was robust at all CARs in cells with the free nuclear BirA in mid-M arrested cells.
source: In contrast, the biotinylation signal was robust at all CARs in cells with the free nuclear BirA.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The majority of cohesins bound to chromosomes are clustering in S phase.
source: In summary, the qPCR and ChIP-seq results suggest that the majority of cohesins bound to chromosomes are clustering in S phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing similar signals between Smc3p-BirA and NLS-BirA conditions in S phase.

claim: In mid-M arrested cells, the presence of cohesin clusters remains high at the centromeres and pericentric regions but is reduced on chromosome arms.
source: In mid-M arrested cells, the presence of clusters remains high at the centromeres and pericentric regions but is reduced on chromosome arms.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The absence of Mcd1p prevents cohesin clustering in G1 and mid-M phases.
source: Thus the absence of Mcd1p prevents cohesin clustering in G1 and mid-M phases, suggesting that Mcd1p is essential for cohesin clustering.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data in Mcd1p-AID depleted cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mcd1p is essential for cohesin clustering.
source: Thus the absence of Mcd1p prevents cohesin clustering in G1 and mid-M phases, suggesting that Mcd1p is essential for cohesin clustering.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of Mcd1p for clustering shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both non-Smc subunits of cohesin (Mcd1p and Scc3p) are required for cohesin clustering.
source: These results suggest that both non-Smc subunits of cohesin are required for cohesin clustering.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data in Scc3p-AID depleted cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Clustering can occur in the absence of cohesion since clusters formed in G1 arrested cells.
source: Furthermore, clustering can occur in the absence of cohesion since clusters formed in G1 arrested cells.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data showing clustering upon Mcd1p overexpression in G1 where cohesion does not occur.

claim: Depletion of Scc2p-AID had no effect on the trans-biotinylation levels seen with either the head or the hinge reporters as compared to wild-type cells.
source: We found that depletion of Scc2p-AID or Eco1p-AID had no effect on the trans-biotinylation levels seen with either the head or the hinge reporters as compared to wild-type cells (Figure 7B, C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Depletion of Eco1p-AID had no effect on the trans-biotinylation levels seen with either the head or the hinge reporters as compared to wild-type cells.
source: We found that depletion of Scc2p-AID or Eco1p-AID had no effect on the trans-biotinylation levels seen with either the head or the hinge reporters as compared to wild-type cells (Figure 7B, C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Neither the loading of cohesin on DNA nor cohesin acetylation is required to form cohesin clusters.
source: These results support four conclusions. Neither the loading of cohesin on DNA nor cohesin acetylation is required to form cohesin clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Scc2p or Eco1p depletion on clustering shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Clustering occurs in the absence of cohesion.
source: Also, clustering occurs in the absence of cohesion as suggested by our experiments analyzing cohesin clusters in G1.
evidence: This is inferred from clustering observed in G1 and in Eco1p-depleted cells where cohesion does not occur.

claim: The presence of cohesin clusters alone is not sufficient to ensure cohesion or condensation in budding yeast.
source: Finally, the presence of cohesin clusters alone is not sufficient to ensure cohesion or condensation in budding yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clustering occurs in conditions where cohesion does not (e.g., Eco1p depletion).

claim: In cells harboring a deletion of WPL1, the biotinylation levels of the head or the hinge reporters were indistinguishable from those observed in the wild-type cells.
source: In cells harboring a deletion of WPL1 (wpl1∆), the biotinylation levels of the head or the hinge reporters were indistinguishable from those observed in the wild-type cells (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Wpl1p is neither an activator nor an inhibitor of clustering.
source: These results suggest that Wpl1p is neither an activator nor an inhibitor of clustering.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Wpl1 deletion on clustering shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Pds5p-AID depletion dramatically reduced the trans-biotinylation levels of both the head and the hinge reporters.
source: In contrast to other regulators, Pds5p-AID depletion dramatically reduced the trans-biotinylation levels of both the head and the hinge reporters (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Pds5p likely promotes the ordered cohesin clustering in mid-M by a mechanism distinct from its functions in promoting cohesin acetylation or cohesin binding to DNA.
source: Therefore, Pds5p likely promotes the ordered cohesin clustering in mid-M by a mechanism distinct from its functions in promoting cohesin acetylation or cohesin binding to DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pds5p depletion blocks clustering but Scc2p and Eco1p depletion do not.

claim: Pds5p promotes clustering of DNA-free as well as DNA-bound cohesin.
source: These results show that Pds5p promotes clustering of DNA-free as well as DNA-bound cohesin.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data in Scc2p and Pds5p co-depleted cells shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Cohesin clusters can be maintained in the absence of Pds5p in S phase.
source: Pds5p-AID depletion in S phase arrested cells had no effect on cohesin clustering as we found the same high levels of biotinylation on both the head and hinge reporters as seen in wild-type cells (Figure 7F, left, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Cohesin clusters require Pds5p to persist post S phase.
source: In contrast, depletion of Pds5p-AID after cells were arrested in mid-M reduced biotinylation of both reporters to basal levels (Figure 7F, right, Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Cohesin clusters can be maintained in the absence of Pds5p in S phase, but they require Pds5p to persist post S phase.
source: These results suggest that cohesin clusters can be maintained in the absence of Pds5p in S phase, but they require Pds5p to persist post S phase.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data showing differential effects of Pds5p depletion in S phase versus mid-M shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The biotinylation patterns observed with double-tagged Smc3p reflect domain interactions within the same cohesin complex.
source: These results suggest that the biotinylation patterns we observed with double-tagged Smc3p reflect domain interactions within the same cohesin complex as we previously suggested.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of biotinylation patterns with and without Pds5p shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The requirement of Pds5p in the maintenance of cohesin clusters correlated with its unusual biological functions to maintain cohesion genome-wide and condensation of the tandemly repeated rDNA locus.
source: The requirement of Pds5p in the maintenance of cohesin clusters correlated with its unusual biological functions to maintain cohesion genome-wide and condensation of the tandemly repeated rDNA locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between Pds5p's role in clustering and its known functions in cohesion and condensation maintenance.

claim: Pds5p-dependent cohesin clustering is necessary for cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that Pds5p-dependent cohesin clustering was necessary for cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between Pds5p's role in clustering and cohesion/condensation maintenance.

claim: Cohesin mutations that specifically block cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation would likely be defective in cohesin clustering.
source: This hypothesis predicts that cohesin mutations that specifically block cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation would likely be defective in cohesin clustering.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that clustering is necessary for cohesion maintenance.

claim: Only three mutations in yeast cohesin are known to cause defects specifically in cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation.
source: Only three mutations in yeast cohesin are known to cause defects specifically in cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation (Eng et al., 2014; Robison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two mutations causing defects specifically in cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation are in Mcd1p, one in the linker (mcd1-V137K) and the other in the ROCC domain (mcd1-Q266).
source: Two mutations are in the Mcd1p, one in the linker (mcd1-V137K) and the other in the regulation of cohesion and condensation (ROCC) domain (mcd1-Q266).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One mutation causing defects specifically in cohesion maintenance and RDN condensation lies in the Smc3p hinge domain (smc3-D667).
source: The third mutation lies in the Smc3p hinge domain (smc3-D667).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All three mutations (mcd1-V137K, mcd1-Q266, smc3-D667) reduced the levels of trans-biotinylation of Smc3p-AviTag reporters by 70%.
source: All three mutations reduced the levels of trans-biotinylation of Smc3p-AviTag reporters by 70%, similar to that seen in Pds5p-depleted cells (Figure 8B, D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that they too were defective for the maintenance of cohesin clusters.
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation data shown in Figure 8B and 8D.

claim: Three domains of cohesin (the Mcd1p linker, Mcd1p ROCC, and Smc3p hinge) are important for cohesin clustering.
source: These results revealed that three domains of cohesin, the Mcd1p linker, Mcd1p ROCC, and Smc3p hinge, are important for cohesin clustering.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of mutations in these domains on clustering shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cohesin clusters on chromosomes are necessary for maintaining cohesion and RDN condensation.
source: Furthermore, these results support the hypothesis that cohesin clusters on chromosomes are necessary for maintaining cohesion and RDN condensation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations blocking clustering also block cohesion maintenance.

claim: Cohesin with mcd1p-V137K binds to chromosomes but fails to bind Pds5p.
source: Cohesin with mcd1p-V137K binds to chromosomes but fails to bind Pds5p (Chan et al., 2013; Eng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Failure of the mcd1-V137K mutated cohesin in clustering suggests that Pds5p must be recruited to chromosome-bound cohesin to promote cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
source: Failure of the mcd1-V137K mutated cohesin in clustering suggests that Pds5p must be recruited to chromosome-bound cohesin to promote cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mcd1-V137K blocks both Pds5p binding and clustering.

claim: Chromosome-bound cohesin molecules with mcd1p-Q266 or smc3p-D667 bind Pds5p.
source: In contrast, chromosome-bound cohesin molecules with mcd1p-Q266 or smc3p-D667 bind Pds5p (Eng et al., 2014; Robison et al., 2018), which suggests that recruitment of Pds5p to cohesin is not sufficient for cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recruitment of Pds5p to cohesin is not sufficient for cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
source: In contrast, chromosome-bound cohesin molecules with mcd1p-Q266 or smc3p-D667 bind Pds5p (Eng et al., 2014; Robison et al., 2018), which suggests that recruitment of Pds5p to cohesin is not sufficient for cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these mutants bind Pds5p but still fail to cluster.

claim: Pds5p is first recruited to cohesin by Mcd1p linker, and then the Mcd1p ROCC region, together with Smc3p hinge domain, promotes cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with a mechanism where Pds5p is first recruited to cohesin by Mcd1p linker, and then the Mcd1p ROCC region, together with Smc3p hinge domain, promotes cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the effects of different mutations on Pds5p binding and clustering.

claim: Cohesin molecules with either version of mutated mcd1p subunit are acetylated to the same level as wild-type cohesin.
source: Finally, cohesin molecules with either version of mutated mcd1p subunit are acetylated to the same level as wild-type cohesin and bind to chromosomes as stably as wild-type cohesin (Eng et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cohesin molecules with either version of mutated mcd1p subunit bind to chromosomes as stably as wild-type cohesin.
source: Finally, cohesin molecules with either version of mutated mcd1p subunit are acetylated to the same level as wild-type cohesin and bind to chromosomes as stably as wild-type cohesin (Eng et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism for cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance is likely independent of any additional functions of these domains in promoting cohesin acetylation and stable binding of cohesin to chromosomes.
source: Thus, the mechanism for cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance is likely independent of any additional functions of these domains in promoting cohesin acetylation and stable binding of cohesin to chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the mutants are acetylated and bind DNA normally but still fail to cluster.

claim: The labeling of multiple AviTags reflects the formation of additional butterfly conformations.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the labeling of multiple AviTags reflects the formation of additional butterfly conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the biotinylation patterns observed in cis-biotinylation experiments.

claim: These multiple conformations may reflect the inherent flexibility of cohesin molecules as their coil coils bend to form the structure shown in EM or additional important intermediates in loop extrusion and/or tethering.
source: These multiple conformations may reflect the inherent flexibility of cohesin molecules as their coil coils bend to form the structure shown in EM or additional important intermediates in loop extrusion and/or tethering.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of multiple conformations.

claim: The formation of multiple distinct butterfly conformations is likely a generic property of SMC complexes as rapid transitions between the ring and multiple butterfly conformations have been observed in recent time-lapse AFM imaging of condensin.
source: The formation of multiple distinct butterfly conformations is likely a generic property of SMC complexes as rapid transitions between the ring and multiple butterfly conformations have been observed in recent time-lapse AFM imaging of condensin (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an AFM study of condensin.

claim: The existence of at least two independent DNA binding activities within cohesin was inferred from genetic experiments and the observation of cohesin's loop extrusion activities.
source: Furthermore, the existence of at least two independent DNA binding activities within cohesin was also inferred from genetic experiments and the observation of cohesin's loop extrusion activities (Eng et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic and loop extrusion studies.

claim: The restriction of DNA binding to the head and hinge domains is likely an intrinsic feature of SMC complexes since AFM images of condensin have shown that DNA is localized to the head and hinge of condensin but not the coiled coil.
source: The restriction of DNA binding to the head and hinge domains is likely an intrinsic feature of SMC complexes since AFM images of condensin have shown that DNA is localized to the head and hinge of condensin but not the coiled coil.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with condensin AFM data.

claim: The existence of butterfly conformations and DNA binding to both the hinge and head domains has been used to propose a scrunching mechanism for loop extrusion by SMC complexes.
source: The existence of butterfly conformations and DNA binding to both the hinge and head domains has been used to propose a scrunching mechanism for loop extrusion by SMC complexes (Ryu et al., 2019; Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study proposing the scrunching mechanism and illustrated in Figure 9A.

claim: Cohesin could be converted from extruding DNA to tethering DNA by blocking the release of ADP from cohesin, thereby trapping an intermediate state in the loop extrusion cycle.
source: We previously suggested that cohesin could be converted from extruding DNA to tethering DNA by blocking the release of Adenosine 5'-diphosphate (ADP) from cohesin, thereby trapping an intermediate state in the loop extrusion cycle (Çamdere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model proposed in a previous study by the authors.

claim: The hinge and head of extended cohesin each could bind a different sister chromatid at or near the DNA replication fork.
source: Here, we speculate that the hinge and head of extended cohesin each could bind a different sister chromatid at or near the DNA replication fork (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is speculation illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: The subsequent formation of the butterfly conformation, cohesin acetylation, and, possibly, association with other factors prevents ADP release that is needed to dissolve the butterfly.
source: The subsequent formation of the butterfly conformation, cohesin acetylation, and, possibly, association with other factors prevents ADP release that is needed to dissolve the butterfly.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of cohesion establishment.

claim: Trapping of the butterfly intermediate prevents additional cycles of scrunching that would release the sister DNA molecule, and as a result, generates a stable tether between sister chromatids.
source: Trapping of this intermediate prevents additional cycles of scrunching that would release the sister DNA molecule, and as a result, generates a stable tether between sister chromatids.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of cohesion establishment.

claim: Cohesin–cohesin interactions on chromosomes in vivo were inferred from functional cooperation between mutated yeast cohesins in vivo.
source: Cohesin–cohesin interactions on chromosomes in vivo were inferred from functional cooperation between mutated yeast cohesins in vivo (Kim et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2008; Eng et al., 2015; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional complementation studies.

claim: A superresolution microscopy study of the worm germline reveals that on the meiotic chromosome axis, meiotic cohesin adopts a conformation that exhibits close proximity between their head and hinge domains.
source: In addition, a superresolution microscopy study of the worm germline reveals that on the meiotic chromosome axis, meiotic cohesin adopts a conformation that exhibits close proximity between their head and hinge domains (Köhler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a superresolution microscopy study.

claim: Cohesin clusters (~4) on meiotic chromosomes.
source: A second study showed that cohesin clusters (~4) on meiotic chromosomes (Woglar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on meiotic cohesin.

claim: The clustering of cohesin butterflies may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic chromosomes.
source: Thus, the clustering of cohesin butterflies may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both yeast and worms.

claim: A role for cohesin clusters in cohesion maintenance is strongly supported by the observation that mutations that specifically fail to maintain cohesin clustering also specifically fail to maintain cohesion.
source: A role for cohesin clusters in cohesion maintenance is strongly supported by the observation that mutations that specifically fail to maintain cohesin clustering (pds5-AID, mcd1-Q266, mcd1-V137K, and smc3-D667) also specifically fail to maintain cohesion (Hartman et al., 2000; Eng et al., 2014; Robison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data in this study and citations to previous studies on cohesion maintenance.

claim: Pds5p-dependent cohesion maintenance is independent of Eco1p and Wpl1p as is the maintenance of cohesion clusters.
source: Furthermore, Pds5p-dependent cohesion maintenance is independent of Eco1p and Wpl1p as is the maintenance of cohesion clusters (Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by data in this study showing clustering is independent of Eco1p and Wpl1p, and by a citation showing Pds5p-dependent cohesion maintenance is independent of these factors.

claim: Pds5p may indirectly promote cluster maintenance by modulating a post-translational modification (other than acetylation by Eco1p) that alters cluster formation or dissolution.
source: Pds5p may indirectly promote cluster maintenance by modulating a post-translational modification (other than acetylation by Eco1p) that alters cluster formation or dissolution.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Pds5p function.

claim: Pds5p may act directly to stabilize clusters by binding to different regions of two adjacent cohesin complexes within the cluster.
source: Alternatively, Pds5p may act directly to stabilize clusters by binding to different regions of two adjacent cohesin complexes within the cluster.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Pds5p function.

claim: Cohesin forms positioned loops genome-wide in mid-M.
source: We recently showed that cohesin forms positioned loops genome-wide in mid-M.
evidence: This is supported by a reference to a recent study by the authors.

claim: Positioned loops continue to form in cells depleted of Pds5p or expressing mcd1p-Q266 where cohesin clustering is blocked.
source: These loops continue to form in cells depleted of Pds5p or expressing mcd1p-Q266 where cohesin clustering is blocked (Costantino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The ability of mutants to loop extrude but not to cluster suggests that cohesin clusters are not obligatory for loop extrusion in vivo.
source: The ability of these mutants to loop extrude but not to cluster suggests that cohesin clusters are not obligatory for loop extrusion in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clustering-defective mutants can still loop extrude.

claim: Cohesin clustering, for example, cohesin dimerization, may modulate its ability to promote symmetric or asymmetric looping.
source: Cohesin clustering, for example, cohesin dimerization, may modulate its ability to promote symmetric or asymmetric looping (Wang et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to loop extrusion studies.

claim: Budding yeast regulates the level and position of clusters on chromosomes.
source: Our study shows that budding yeast also regulates the level and position of clusters on chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing cell cycle-regulated changes in cluster distribution.

claim: Clusters occur in S phase at all previously identified sites of cohesin binding (centromeres, pericentromeric regions, and the many CARs along chromosome arms).
source: The ChIP experiment results with trans-biotinylated cohesin suggest that clusters occur in S phase at all previously identified sites of cohesin binding (centromeres, pericentromeric regions, and the many CARs along chromosome arms).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In mid-M, clusters are specifically reduced at arm CARs.
source: In mid-M, clusters are specifically reduced at arm CARs (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5D and illustrated in Figure 9C.

claim: The reduction in arm clusters likely leads to a reduction in the robustness of arm cohesion in mid-M.
source: This reduction in arm clusters likely leads to a reduction in the robustness of arm cohesion in mid-M, given the correlation between the cohesin clustering and cohesion maintenance (this study).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between clustering and cohesion maintenance.

claim: The reduction of arm cohesion occurs in mammalian prophase by WAPL-dependent destabilization of cohesin binding to DNA.
source: Interestingly, the reduction of arm cohesion also occurs in mammalian prophase by WAPL-dependent destabilization of cohesin binding to DNA (Kueng et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on mammalian cohesin.

claim: The reduction of arm cohesion is likely a conserved feature of mitosis.
source: Thus, the reduction of arm cohesion is likely a conserved feature of mitosis (albeit by different mechanisms).
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both yeast and mammals.

claim: Proper mitotic chromosome segregation requires the establishment and maintenance of tension that results from the bipolar attachment of sister kinetochores and the surrounding cohesion.
source: Proper mitotic chromosome segregation requires the establishment and maintenance of tension that results from the bipolar attachment of sister kinetochores and the surrounding cohesion (Makrantoni and Marston, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on chromosome segregation.

claim: Cohesion around the centromere may be strengthened by the cohesin clusters, helping the tension to persist after bipolar attachment.
source: This cohesion may be strengthened by the cohesin clusters around the centromere, helping the tension to persist after bipolar attachment (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is speculation illustrated in Figure 9C.

claim: In C. elegans, COH-3/COH-4 cohesins are remodeled prior to anaphase I of meiosis, persisting primarily distal to the crossover.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, COH-3/COH-4 cohesins are remodeled prior to anaphase I of meiosis, persisting primarily distal to the crossover (Severson and Meyer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on C. elegans meiotic cohesin.

claim: COH-3/COH-4 cohesins form clusters.
source: Interestingly, imaging data suggest that COH-3/COH-4 cohesins form clusters.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data, likely from the cited study.

claim: Cohesin clusters may serve to strengthen cohesion and facilitate the persistence of tension in meiosis.
source: These clusters may also serve to strengthen cohesion and facilitate the persistence of tension.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of clusters in meiosis.

claim: The regulation of cluster persistence in the genome may be a conserved feature of eukaryotes that is important for proper sister chromatid and homolog alignment in both meiosis and mitosis.
source: Thus, the regulation of cluster persistence in the genome may be a conserved feature of eukaryotes that is important for proper sister chromatid and homolog alignment in both meiosis and mitosis.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations in multiple organisms.
